title: The role of restraint in fatal excited delirium: A research synthesis and pooled analysis

claims.statement: 'Excited delirium' is a contested label rather than a recognized diagnosis, and evidence is insufficient to say whether the state it describes kills without restraint, or how far deaths given the label were caused by restraint, by drugs such as cocaine, or by both. It is not in the international classification of diseases (ICD) or the psychiatric manual (DSM), has no validated diagnostic criteria and no autopsy or laboratory finding specific to it, and is applied as a diagnosis of exclusion, mainly in medico-legal reports of deaths of agitated people during or after police restraint or in custody (Gonçalves Dias & Cainé, 2026; Strömmer et al., 2020). In the published case literature the label was used mostly by forensic pathologists, and also by emergency physicians and others, and a 2012 defining review and a 2009 emergency physicians' white paper gave fatality figures for it (under 10% and 8.3%) that the authors of the pooled analysis below trace to a study without any death figures (Strömmer et al., 2020). The authors of both reviews read here reject the term: one team proposes 'agitated delirium' with a note of the presence and degree of restraint, and recording the manner of death of restrained people as homicide or undetermined rather than natural or accident (Strömmer et al., 2020); the other uses 'acute behavioral disturbance' and reports critics' view that the label deflects attention from restraint and is applied with racial bias (Gonçalves Dias & Cainé, 2026). In a pooled analysis of 168 published cases (English-language case reports and series to April 2020), 92 of 120 cases labelled 'excited delirium' had died, against 12 of 48 labelled 'agitated delirium'; some force, from manual restraint and handcuffs to electrical weapons or sedation, was recorded in 94 of the 104 deaths, only 3 of the 168 cases had no force recorded (2 of them died), and cocaine was noted in 55 of the 104 deaths and 19 of the 64 survivors, as the case reports described it rather than as toxicology results (Strömmer et al., 2020). Its authors read this as no evidence that excited delirium kills without restraint; but their own introduction notes that forensic reports describe deaths and use 'excited delirium' while clinical reports describe survivors, so the label, death and the recording of restraint travel together by type of source, which the analysis did not take into account, and the authors later corrected one table (Strömmer et al., 2020, and the first reader's appraisal). A 2026 systematic review of deaths in custody (searches for 2010 to 2025) describes restraint deaths mostly in young or middle-aged men, often with obesity and stimulant intoxication, names cocaine, methamphetamine and phencyclidine as 'frequently identified in toxicological analyses' without figures, favours breathing restriction and metabolic collapse during face-down restraint over a heart-rhythm death driven by stimulants while allowing the latter in some deaths, and reports, without figures, that restraint-related deaths are under-recorded in official statistics; in one Ontario series of 46 investigation reports, most deaths were classified as accidental or natural (Gonçalves Dias & Cainé, 2026). Both reviews are rated critically low for their methods, neither counts how often drugs caused or contributed to these deaths, and neither can show the cause of any single death. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
claims.magnitude: Not estimable. Pooled published cases (n = 168): died 104 (61.9%); 92/120 labelled 'excited delirium' against 12/48 'agitated delirium' (unadjusted odds ratio 9.9); some force recorded in 94/104 deaths, none in 2, unknown in 8; no force recorded in 3 of 168 cases (2 fatal); police first on the scene 95/120 against 16/48; cocaine noted in 55/104 deaths and 19/64 survivors; fatal share 90% of 30 cases published before 2000 and 56% of 138 published 2000–2020. Second-hand figures cited by the 2026 review: Finland 12 restraint-associated deaths among 21,036 autopsies (0.06%); 229 deaths, 58% within 1–5 minutes of starting face-down restraint; Ontario, 46 investigation reports, most classed accidental or natural. No counts of drug involvement.
